utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Can we have the case called, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Brdjanin. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Ackerman. Appearances for General Talic. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Xavier de Roux and Natasha Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we start with the witness, two very short matters. Mr. Ackerman and Maitre de Roux, you are aware, because I'm sure you have been served with a copy of the Prosecutor's memo in compliance with a directive of this Chamber re-justification for the delay, nondisclosure of the identity of a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you speaking of a motion that might have been filed within the last couple of days maybe?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Friday, I think. Yeah, the end of last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I'll be writing -- I'll be filing a written response to that, Your Honour. I oppose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And Maitre de Roux? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Yes, we received it Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And will you be responding? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] No. We haven't responded yet, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But will you be filing a response? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] I give the floor to Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we do not object to this motion, but under the condition that between the date of the communication of the identity of the witness and the date that the appearance of this witness, there should be two weeks without trial so that we can go to Bosnia and conduct our investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I would suppose that you're going to file a written response, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is not sufficient to you, then we will file a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I would expect it. I mean, if this is what you're requesting, obviously it should be put on record in a more formal manner. So that will be -- Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, all I would say about this is we complied with Your Honours' ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I put it this way: It was slightly unusual but I take that Your Honour would be applying the same standards or rules to the Defence if they do the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we handed down or we gave that order for a very simple reason. And you find it in --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We read the judgement, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean, there has been already a decision by Judge Hunt in this case which we think ought to be followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ought to be followed obviously applicable to both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. If it's applicable to both sides, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, we nearly did discuss the fact that Judge Hunt's order actually relates to a different situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But if it's to be applied across the board, then Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It will be applied across the board, but although the case was somewhat different -- or the circumstances somewhat different, the principle remains the same. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me just say, Your Honour, that there will never come a time in this case when I will seek your permission not to disclose the name of a witness to the Prosecutor, because counsel need to know who the witnesses are going to be. The purpose of the rules regarding witness protection are to protect the witnesses from public knowledge of their identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Let's not argue -- let's not argue about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... responsibilities in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My intervention was meant only to get to know whether to expect a response negative, positive, or whatever. The next thing I wanted to make sure of is that you are prepared for tomorrow's informal meeting, which will take place in room 177 at 11.00 a.m. I have -- a preliminary meeting has already been held between the senior legal officer together with the rest of my staff in preparation for this meeting, and tomorrow morning I will have a meeting myself with Mr. Von Hebel to make sure that everything is -- is in place. During the meeting -- and I have already asked my legal assistant to approach you in an informal manner. It is desirable that there will be some discussion, and preferably also some agreement on possible agreed facts. So you will be approached for -- with this aim in view by my -- today I think during the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've been handed it already, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Please do give this matter your utmost attention. Obviously it's in the Chamber's interest to secure it. None of us approaches this matter suspecting that you are being invited to compromise your position. The idea is where there are facts that could be agreed upon, which are either neutral or which does not affect your client in any way, as well as the Prosecution obviously, probably if you could reach an agreement on that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is entirely a matter for the Defence. Obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll wish to have agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And having said that, I think we can start with the -- continue with the witness. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I kindly ask you to make the solemn declaration once more, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. You may sit down. Ms. Korner will be continuing her examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry. Just before we go on with that, Your Honour will recall there was a question yesterday about this village --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Which you had to check out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two villages, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember what the first village was now. The second village was -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The village was Kasapnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Kasapnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What we've taken -- I've spoken to Mr. Inayat about this obviously, who produced these maps, and we've only got one copy of it. But there's a map produced of Sanski Most by the Bosnians themselves, showing the ethnic composition. It may not matter very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if it is important. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It shows -- and I think perhaps I can deal with it best this way, that it -- it shows that Kljevci was a Serb village and Kasapnica was supposed to be a suburb of this. But perhaps the best thing I can do is show the witness the original Bosnian map and then just ask him about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's -- if it's the only copy that you have, Ms. Korner, let's put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. If the witness can have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the witness can either look on the monitor or directly on the document itself

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir, can I just ask you, have you seen one of these types of maps before?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map, it is possible that I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday that Kasapnica was a village without any Serbs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is it in fact close to a hamlet of Kljevci?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But from your knowledge -- which is a Serb village, I think.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kljevci, one part of it is a Serb village. That's correct. Kasapnica was a locality of a mass grave, a location of a mass grave. It's an abandoned hamlet of Kljevci, where Croats used to live before. And the wider locality is called Kljevci.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, then, this is clearly the evidence. And although it's marked like that, everybody has heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we can take it off the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you intend tendering that document as an exhibit? I don't think it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Unless anybody wants it as an exhibit, I wouldn't have thought so -- no, I see heads shaking all round.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, can we go back to where we finished yesterday, and you were talking about the 6th Krajina Brigade and the mobilisation that took place. In fact -- I'm sorry. You will need the map we produced back again for a moment, which is Exhibit -- no, no. The proper exhibit, 757.2. Sir, I want to ask you about JNA training fields in the area. I think it's right that there were no actual barracks in the region of Sanski Most. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. There were no barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did it have various training grounds in the area or near Sanski Most, first of all in a place called Lusci Palanka?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 6th Sanski Brigade had training ground in the area of Lusci Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which we can see, I think, on the map marked towards the left-hand corner, or the left-hand side, rather. And how far was that from the town of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lusci Palanka is about 25 kilometres away from the town approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think it's going in the direction of the municipality of Bosanski Krupa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then the next training ground, was that in a place called Koprivna, which we can see near the River Sana towards the middle -- right-hand side of the map?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Koprivna is on the way between Sanski Most towards the airport. It's about 3 or 4 kilometres distance away from the town. And in this area, there were units of the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And after returning -- returning from Croatia, from the Republic of Croatia, after returning from the front, there were some battalions that were stationed there, and they also had manoeuvres.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did that in fact give them control of the road towards Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then was there -- were there further training grounds at Kruhari, which we can see very close to the right-hand side as we look at the map of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kruhari were also stationed some battalions that belonged to the 6th Krajina Brigade, under a certain command. And this was used for training before the beginning of the attack on Sanski Most from the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, were there also training grounds in the vicinity of a place called Dabar? We can see it marked on the map below Sanski Most. I think it's Gornji Dabar and Donji Dabar, and were there training grounds there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I'll explain that Dabar is south-west from the town of the Sanski Most. These are hills, and going towards Grmic, Mount Grmec. It's a very large area which the 6th Krajina Brigade occupied and set out their positions -- set up their positions. Specifically in Magarice which is a part above the town towards Dabar. That's where also the HQ was with the commander Colonel of the JNA Branko Basara. In Dabar -- so before the beginning of the attack on Sanski Most, for days there were detonations of cannon shells that could be heard. Towards Dabar in April and May --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Don't worry. I'm going to come to April and May. I'm just trying to establish where the grounds are at the moment.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And finally, was there a further training ground at a place called Milin Birt. And I'm not sure that's marked on the map. Could you indicate where that was roughly.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milin Birt is located also on the main road between Sanski Most and Prijedor. And it is about 2 or 3 kilometres away from the town. It is a crossroads of regional road which separates -- which goes off to the left towards a large Muslim settlement, Stari Majdan, then to the Croatian settlement, Stara Rijeka, and it also goes to Ljubija, which is the municipality of Prijedor. On the crossroads, there was a large checkpoint of the military place of the 6th Krajina Brigade, and a brigade -- or rather, the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it was the military police who were there.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where the police -- the military police was as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So is it -- can he -- can the witness point it on the map for us. Is it past Stara Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think he said it was past Stari Majdan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, past Stari Majdan, past Stara Rijeka. If you can mark it with a pen on the same map and then put your initials, please. We need to have it on the ELMO so that we can see from here as well, please. He can mark it now, but then we need to see it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I apologise. Let me just get my bearings. So from Podbrijezje, in the immediate vicinity is a hamlet marked here Podbrijezje, and I'll put a blue dot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Cross it with an "X", please, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because we have several blue dots.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. But didn't you mention it before that it was in the direction of Stari Majdan and Stara Rijeka? That's further up. No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So where you have marked with an "X," what does that "X" represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is approximately the location, the place called Milin Birt. You pass through Podbrijezje and then just behind Podbrijezje in the direction of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what was the name again?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was Milin Birt.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's two words.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was looking at the bottom of page 4 of the statement, and you'll see the name there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to move now, please, to what happened after the war in Croatia broke out in Sanski Most. What was the attitude towards the inhabitants of Sanski Most who were of Croat ethnicity? What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the war in Croatia started, the Croatian population in Sanski Most was in an unfavourable situation because, if I can put it this way, the Serb representatives through the policies of the SDS expressed themselves very -- in a very negative way about the Croats in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you just describe to us, please, the physical manifestation of that negative way. What was actually happening to the Croats?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what happened was that there was a series of terrorist activities against citizens of Croatian nationality at that time in Sanski Most. For instance, in the settlement of Kruhari, which was a mixed village with Serbs and Croats, there were some bombs that were set to explode, there were even some murders. There were grenades that were thrown on houses. And I would say that a -- that there was a terror of a very cunning type that was being exerted on the Croatian population. And this was the same situation in other villages where Croats lived. So somewhere in Ovanjska near Budimlic Japra, a Croat was killed, and his house was set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you as an investigating judge investigate many of these incidents?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an investigating judge, I went to do the investigation in the case of all these explosions and terrorist attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever find materials, items that had been used to cause the explosions?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. On all these occasions, I would find parts of devices -- of explosive devices -- hand grenades, rifle grenades, and remnants of explosives.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you able to identify the origin of these explosives in the sense of where they came from?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was. More or less in all cases I was able to identify the origin --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of the explosive device. And I can say that these were lethal means coming from the stockpiles of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how are you able to say that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the jackets of the rifle grenades and on the remnants of those grenades, I was able to tell the origin of the explosive device. Also in the case of hand grenades I could see that they were grenades manufactured in a military factory of Yugoslavia that was situated in Bugojno. So on the basis of the remnants of that grenade, I was able to tell the origin. My task as the investigating judge is to investigate and to prosecute the perpetrators. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't -- I think you explained that. All I -- because I need to move through, sir.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry about that. What I want to know about this finally -- this matter finally is this: Were you ever -- was anybody ever arrested and prosecuted for any of these bombings or explosive attacks?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whose duty was it to arrest these people or to order the arrest, yours as an investigating judge or the police's?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first place, it is the duty of the police to identify the perpetrators, that is, people for whom there are grounds to suspect them of having committed the crime, and to report this to the prosecutor and the judge. Not in a single case was such a perpetrator identified, because of which I intervened on a number of occasions and objected very seriously about it to the chief of police and to the head of the crimes department in Sanski Most. And both of them were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, still staying in 1991 -- and I'm going to move shortly to 1992. Were there any such attacks on Muslim persons or property?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period of time, there were still no such attacks on Muslims and Muslim property. This would occur later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, in 1991 were there rallies held in the Sanski Most area on behalf of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember some rallies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you remember -- firstly, did you attend any of those rallies?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present at one rather large organised rally in the square in the centre of town, which was organised by the SDS of Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you remember, first of all, who the speakers were, or some of them?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the speakers were the leaders of the SDS of Sanski Most municipality. I don't remember any other persons from outside Sanski Most. But I do remember most groups that would come to that meeting or rally carrying Chetnik banners and Chetnik insignia, wearing beards. I also remember some speeches by Rasula and Vrkes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In general terms, what was the tone of the speeches, the theme?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The danger that the Serb people were in and a call for the unity of the Serb people, the -- even then I felt the tendency to create a unified state in order to preserve Serbdom within a single state.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we move then to 1992. In February of 1992, was the referendum -- I'm sorry. Before -- I beg your pardon. Before we leave 1991, was there a referendum held by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A plebiscite of the Serb people was organised. That is how they called it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you have anything to do with the organisation or any monitoring of that particular plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I had nothing to do with it, because I wasn't invited, even though officially I was the president of the municipal elections commission elected to that position at the assembly meeting of Sanski Most municipality. And I did have the qualifications.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, in 1992, however, was the referendum held to decide upon the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you involved in the organisation of that referendum through your official position?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, as the president of the municipal elections commission, it was my task to provide professional assistance in accordance with the law and the constitution to organize and implement the referendum in the Sanski Most municipality, which I in fact did, together with the other members of the commission coming from the ranks of the Bosniak and Croat people, because members of the municipal SM commission from the Serb ethnic group decided not to participate in the work of the commission. However, we had a sufficient number of seven members and we carried it out in accordance with the law and the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, what I want to ask you about that: We know what the results were overall, but were there any particular problems that you had with the positioning of polling stations in Serb areas?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We organised the referendum and covered the whole area with polling stations so as not to provoke any anger among the Serb people. However, on the eve of the referendum itself, from the territory of the settlement of Tomina, I received a written ultimatum saying that in that area, there would be no referendum in the premises of the local offices which we had chosen as a polling station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who gave you that ultimatum? Who did the written ultimatum come from?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That ultimatum was in written form, as I have just said. It was brought in person by the secretary -- active secretary from Tomina, Toma Renovic [phoen], who was in the local branch of the SDS in charge of Tramosnja and Tomina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As a result of that ultimatum, what did you do about the polling station? Did you leave it there, or did you move it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I immediately convened a meeting of the commission, and we agreed to move the station, even though those were -- that was an office belonging to the Sanski Most municipality as the -- as a communal office. And we moved the polling station to a Bosniak home in Tomina. If I may, I would like to add something.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a polling station for the area of Begici settlement, which is in Kljevci, and we designated as a polling station there the home of a Bosniak, Ceric Miralem. That's a correction on my part. Not Begic, but Ceric. However, on the 31st of May, 1992, this old man, who was about 70, and his younger son and his older son were killed on the bridge at Vrhpolje. Afterwards his wife was dead too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that one of the bodies that was exhumed later on?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did exhume some bodies. But their death is linked to the positions of the polling station in that house. That house was totally destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, at the time of this referendum and before the referendum was held, what was the attitude of the SDS and the Serbs towards this referendum, as it was expressed through speeches or leaflets or posters?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. We are not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. She failed to switch on her microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we're all guilty of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you repeat once more what you have just said stated, please, for our benefit, because we were not receiving interpretation into English. I'm sorry about that, Judge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The SDS of Sanski Most municipality worked in an organised manner against the referendum in Sanski Most by leaflets that were posted on various institutions, in the halls of buildings, which appeared one morning. And it was stated in these leaflets propaganda to the effect that the referendum was directed against the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was the language like in those leaflets?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wording was horrific. Mostly to the effect that the Muslims and Croats would, let me say, kill Serb children, that they would destroy the Serb people. They made mention of the name of Alija Izetbegovic. And simply in that leaflet, the Serbs were appealed upon not to vote in the referendum and not to allow the referendum to be organised in the area or in the local communes inhabited by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I just want you to have -- I want to -- although I want to look at the documents in one bunch, as it were, I want you to look, please, at one particular document, which is Exhibit P700.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If that could be handed to the witness, but just one part of it. And I would like to have a look at the B/C/S. And if Your Honours would have a look at it, because the translation doesn't reveal what this is. No, I'm sorry, usher. Could you give it to me. I just want to look at one single part of it. It's just easier if I just find it. Thanks. I want the witness to see it, please. Sorry. No, it's my fault. If we look in our bundles at the third page of that translation, headed "Dear brother Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, is that document you're looking at, does that say "Dear brother Serbs" at the top?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That's what it said. This leaflet is similar to the other leaflet, but it is on half a page. But the text in the leaflet is similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just very quickly look at the text --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Although Your Honours will recall I read part of this in opening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Dear brother Serbs, do you know what our blood thirsty enemies have been scheming for us? What they had in mind was to gouge out our eyes, carve us up, hack our bodies to piece, rape women and girls in front of their dearest, to circumcise, to destroy our religion, to crush us just because we happen to be Serbs. Don't think that anybody's family would have been spared. They had monstered ready committed to raping Serbian women and they had developed a system of killing each and every Serb. Soon we will show everyone their horrible weapons, the Serb cutter, swords from the middle-ages, sledge hammers, special knives, instruments to gouge out eyes out with, and instruments to carve us up with." And then the rest -- it's clear this was written a little later because it refers to Vrhpolje. Now, first of all, is this the sort of language that was being used in the leaflets that were being distributed before the referendum?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely such a leaflet was distributed even to homes, apartments. I know that a leaflet of this content was read out over the Serb radio Sanski Most on the 27th of May, 1992, because I heard it with my own ears in the prison in which I was detained, in the immediate vicinity of the public security station. This leaflet was all read -- read all day long and maybe the following days as well and was the most important propaganda material they used. I think that someone recorded this on an audiotape and that this audio recording is in the possession of the Prosecution, recorded from the Serb radio over which it was broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to answer -- I'm sorry. I just want to ask you this. And if you can't answer it, say so straight away. Do you know whether ordinary Serbs believed this is what the Muslims wanted to do to them? Did you speak to anybody about what was being said? If you don't know the answer, as I say, say so straight away.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need more time to explain this, because I was simply in a state of shock. I couldn't believe that people with whom I had socialised, worked, and was a good friend with could suddenly turn their backs on me. However, the impression I got that day when the attack on Sanski Most started, that -- it's hard to describe it as a collective turning of heads away. I think that many people were misled and that they simply didn't dare react. Maybe later on I will be able to tell you that I spoke to some of my friends when I received a threatening letter before my arrest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we'll come on to the letter you received, as you say, when we reach that part. All right. Can we move -- the referendum was held. And the vote not participated in by Serbs was a majority for independence. After that referendum, what was the attitude towards the Muslim and Croat population in the area of Sanski Most from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the referendum, there was a lot of tension in relationships already then. When I was sending reports on the referendum to Sarajevo, I noticed that there was some movement of groups of Serb ethnicity, about which I later learned that they were members of the SOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Again, can I -- I want to deal with the SOS as a -- a concrete topic. But just generally, you explained that there were explosions directed against Croats when the war broke out. Did that -- did those explosions and attacks extend to the Muslims after the referendum?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. Precisely at that time frequent terrorist attacks occurred on buildings, businesses in Sanski Most, of mining, of the setting of explosive devices, of destruction of facilities, buildings in the surrounding area of Sanski Most which belonged to Bosniaks. There were even attacks, armed attacks, in rural areas. For instance, on the crossroads of Milin Birt, the military patrol -- an army patrol which had the crossroads under its control fired from automatic weapons at a vehicle where a Bosniak young man was killed. Also on the road from Budimlic Japra towards Sanski Most, a Bosniak, a teacher was attacked who was returning from work in a vehicle. And he was also fired at with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly when this was?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in April and May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you try and conduct any sort of investigation into those incidents?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a judge, I went into the field and I would conduct an investigation and I would seek for an investigation to be opened. But as I have already explained before, not one such activity was uncovered by the members of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say that there was this incident in which a military patrol opened fire on a vehicle and that the Bosniak was killed. Did you have any dealings with the military over this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will have to correct myself. This Bosniak was severely injured in his spine, and he is a severely disabled invalid. Fortunately he did survive. And now I'm going to answer your question. I was on the scene of the incident; that is, I was at the command post of that unit. And I had a conversation regarding how the incident occurred. At that time I became convinced that this was done without any reason because this young man, accompanied by a friend, was actually living in Milin Birt, and he was coming from the direction of Sanski Most going towards his home.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about the actual circumstances of what happened. All that I want to know about is this: Were you allowed to interview any of the people who were allegedly responsible for the shooting?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As they were members of the military, did they come under your jurisdiction or the jurisdiction of the military court?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were under the jurisdiction of military courts, because they were members of the 6th Krajina Brigade, which was still at that time was part of the JNA, that is, of the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not any steps were taken to prosecute these men, whether any charges were brought?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not charged, nor were any steps undertaken. Although, it is known perfectly well who opened fire on the crossroad.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I move from that. Those were two incidents that you described. You mentioned now the SOS. Can you tell us, when you first became aware of a group calling itself the Serbian defence forces or SOS.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard for me to define precisely at the time, but I can say that I first heard about some secret Serb organisation who were civilians and that they were rather prone to criminal behaviour, to setting up of explosives, mining, provoking disorder. I knew most of these people. I then learnt that they had a military vehicle, and I saw that vehicle. This vehicle comes from the JNA. It is a lorry. I don't know whether they had one or two. On the door of the driver's cabin, on both sides, left and right, it was written in Cyrillic alphabet "SOS." SOS. This lorry or lorries had a canvas back to start with. Later on in April, the canvas back was taken off, and then I saw them more frequently patrolling around the town or going to areas of other localities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Then when -- when they started to dismiss managers and directors in organs, institutions, companies, that's when the SOS, or rather, the SOS members were always present, on those occasions, together with Rasula and with Vlado Vrkes. So with my own eyes, I saw the occasion when the director of the public auditing service was forced out, Mrs. Ankica Dobrijevic. They physically forced their entrance into the premises and they physically removed her from the premises.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to come again to dismissals as a discrete topic. But can I just go over a couple of the things you said. First, you say you knew most of these people. Were these people in uniform or in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you say you knew them, were they local people then?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were people from Sanski Most. Most of them I knew. And at first, there were about 30 to 50 of them, perhaps 40.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what sort of people were they? I mean, obviously I assume they were men. But what sort of reputation did these people have?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mostly problematic persons, meaning their behaviour. I can say that they were criminals, in fact. And I think that they were specially selected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you said that they were prone to criminal behaviour, they set explosives, they provoked disorder. Did the police make any attempt to control them?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never, because at that time from the referendum until my arrest they were some kind of force in the town. They were terrorising the town. They provoked fear among the population. And every night they were blowing up a building belonging to Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about attacks on people? Did they carry out attacks on people as well?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. They also attacked people. On one occasion, I was in a situation when a teacher called me on the phone, a secondary schoolteacher from the Sanski Most grammar school. His name was Blaz Grgic. He was a teacher of German. He told me that his apartment had been broken into and that he had been robbed, that he was robbed of a large sum of money that he had, and he was -- and he told me that this was done by two persons whose names were Dusan Saovic aka Njunja and Dusan Mudrinic, aka Medeni. Who already then were feared in town, together with other members of that group. He did not dare report it to the police, that is, to the police at that time. So I called him to come to me, and I interviewed him. After that interview, I had reasonable grounds to believe that these persons did commit this offence. I then reported this to the police, and I ordered for this to be investigated. However, the following day, that is -- yes, the following day, they went into the school centre, to the school with weapons. They were armed. And they attacked the teacher, who was then forced to flee, he then had to flee Sanski Most, either the next day or the following days. I would also like to add that due to the terror that was continually present and that was also increasing in intensity, the population, the Bosniaks and the Croats, were leaving the Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to stop here for the time being, Ms. Korner, for a quarter of an hour. And we will resume immediately after.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We're having a break, Judge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I see you standing, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are problems with regard to the diary that I just have no idea how we're going to solve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you informed Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. We have been talking about it today. What they did -- and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, I thought it was too good to be true, no problems today. I mean, it's quite unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Ms. Korner didn't do this. It was somebody on her staff that did it. But what they did was they gave us a list of those portions of the diary that had not yet been set to translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You explained yourself yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That they would send a translation. So we were working on it this morning. And what that requires is that we take the translation that we've got so far and sit down with what they say they have additionally sent and try to figure out by comparing what has been translated and what hasn't, what it was they decided to leave out. I thought that would be a simple thing to solve. When I same this morning, I said, "Just give us the page numbers of what you decided not to send for translation so we can then look at those and decide if we agree." And that was kind of the agreement that we had made, that they would show us what they thought should not be translated, and then we would have -- have an opportunity to say yes or no about that. It turns out that it cannot be reconstructed at this point. They cannot tell us what it was they decided not to send for translation. That's what I was just told a little -- a few moments ago. So I think there are two possibilities: I think it would take us, the two of us -- one of my assistants who speaks the language and I are sitting down going through this, it would probably take us a couple of weeks to extract those thing that have not been sent for translation. The other possibility is to revert back to Judge Hunt's order and have it all translated. But there's no way to solve the problem that has arisen now that I can think of. Maybe you can think of one, Judge. You sometimes are a great deal smarter than me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not immediately. Not until I have heard the other side. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, we have indicated of the untranslated bits, those numbers that Your Honours have seen, it is called the ERN numbers, so that it's quite easy to sort out which pages we haven't sent for translation of the yet untranslated material. In effect -- and Your Honour, this is quite simple -- we asked them to translate the parts between August and -- April and September 1992, and that was done. And then there was the request for the rest of that year. So all that has to be done is for them to check the page numbers from January 1992 through to, I think we said, the 4th of April, and then the September ones. And all they've got to see is the page numbers that we haven't sent for translation. May I say the selection of none translation was -- in fact, it was Mr. Ackerman or maybe Madam Fauveau who brought it to my attention -- was there are parts where the diarist refers to squirrels running across the garden and that sort of stuff and we decided that really wasn't relevant, and to so that was extracted. I'd be surprised if we'd extracted anything that didn't relate to events. The second matter is this: The one thing that we all tried to do is to save the Translation Unit having to translate things which really are not relevant. We all know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They're extremely, busy, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That they're overwhelmed. And therefore -- I hear Mr. Ackerman saying two weeks to sort this out. I would have thought to simply sit down for a day, it would achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. I believed exactly what Ms. Korner just said when I spoke to you yesterday. And we carried out exactly the exercise she talks about this morning. What we did was we looked at one of the things that they said they had sent for translation. It has particular ERN numbers. We can then look up the B/C/S version that has those ERN numbers. And when you do that, you find that there are parts of it that appear not to have been sent for translation because they're not included within the page range. So then you look at that, and it contains material that obviously should have been translated. And then when you do a search of the translated material, you find that it actually was sent for translation. So it has been translated. So what I originally thought when we were working on it this morning was that there was a great deal of what I would call exculpatory material that they had decided not to send for translation, but it turns out that it was translated as an earlier time. And the only way to find out what has not been sent for translation is to really make a -- an almost word-for-word comparison with the Serbian version and the English version sitting side by side. Because what Ms. Korner suggests on using the ERN numbers gets you nowhere. It only gets you what was sent for translation in this batch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, what I am going to do, Mr. Ackerman, for the time being is -- And perhaps you could pass on the message to Mr. Von Hebel who will get in touch with me tomorrow on this. I am going to give instructions to the senior legal officer to include this on the agenda for tomorrow's meeting so that you can actually discuss it in his presence, and if possible, if you have any documents that you might bring along or carry along with you tomorrow to show to Mr. Von Hebel to explain exactly where the problem lies, I think that would help. And then after that, I will discuss it with him and see how best to tackle this problem. I think for the time being, that's what we ought to do. I think you ought to have with you the same report that you handed to me. And also if possible, if these exist, there is a bundle of documents -- pages from this diary that have not been translated and are not going to be translated which you can produce tomorrow, I think you would help Mr. Von Hebel tremendously to be able to take stock of how really problematic this -- how much of a problem this really is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Judge, if they could hand me the page that is they have decided not to send for translation, that would end the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe this is why -- this is why I am mentioning. Because if they exist, they are already in a bundle, that would solve the problem, except that you may still come forward and say, "We are not quite sure that this is all it."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There may be others. We still have to compare the B/C/S with the English, one page after another, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. But in any case, let's deal with it first the way I am indicating, and then we'll see afterwards. Yes, Maitre --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand, but the reason I rose to address you is that I was informed that there is no such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe the Prosecution don't have them. Maybe the translation -- Translation Unit have already put them aside. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can tell you -- well, I see Maitre de Roux on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Maitre de Roux. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do not want to prolong this debate. I already said what I thought of this matter. This is a -- an eternal problem of quotations and a selection of quotations. We either have all the documents or we have just quotations from documents. And I believe that in a case which is so serious, it is important to have the entire context of every document so that we are able to read it, so that we are able to understand what this diary is trying to say in its entirety, rather than have extracts from here and there and quotations which are either exculpatory or they're helping to convict. So I believe that the Prosecution, if they want to use a document, I believe that it will be fair for everyone to know its entirety and its whole context.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm tempted to say to that that Madam Fauveau can spend a happy evening reading through this diary in its entirety. However, we have a duty not to overload the translation department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a question of a duty only, Ms. Korner. I was going to -- I mean, I was trying to restrain myself from mentioning it, but there has been developments in the field of what ought to be translated. And if not entirely, a scale of prioritising translation by -- translations by the responsible -- by the unit responsible for translations. And you know, or you should know as much -- when I say "you," it's not you, Ms. Korner, it's everyone. You all should be in a position to know that this matter has been taken up by the bureau and certain decisions taken, which necessarily if I am to apply them or if we are to apply them necessarily have a bearing on what has been decided previously, both in this case and in other cases, as to what should be translated. In other words -- I don't want to carry this much further if there is a practical solution to it. But if there is no practical solution to it, I will definitely have to revise the -- first review and then revise the position and act in accordance with what has already been decided administratively, internally as to what should be translated and what should be translated first before -- before the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say that we're -- I'm going to see what we can do. It -- I said to Mr. Ackerman earlier before Your Honour came in that this was all on the basis that in future, he would also tell us not what he hadn't done but whatever. But -- but Your Honour, I'll see if there's anything we can do to solve this problem by tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do. And I am entrusting you in the hands of Mr. Von Hebel because I know what a valid person he is, and I'm sure that having heard both of you and possibly seen some -- seen firsthand some of the documents which you may have, he probably will come with some practical solution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it will certainly give us something to discuss at this conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And we also have to our advantage that there is ample time between now and September, because that's the month you mentioned yesterday or the day before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's when they're going to complete the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have ample time within which we can manoeuvre and find the practical solution. Yes. Sorry, Judge. I'm sure that in your court this happens as well. We can now proceed with the cross-examination -- with the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, all I'm going to do -- and I think these maps may be useful to Your Honours in future, because there are proper ordnance survey types.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask that the witness just have a look at one map which I've marked in yellow because I think that's where the Milin Birt is and just confirm it, and then I'll hand it up to yourself also -- and to my learned friends also marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to ask you whether they have a legend, but they do. I can see it from here. Because otherwise -- otherwise it may not be easy for everyone to read.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No sir, I'll tell you what -- can you just -- sir, if you look at that, I've marked a place in yellow highlighter. I wonder how you translate that. But can you just confirm that that's Milin Birt that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the locality. It can be seen very well on this map. It is north, north-west in relation to the town of Sanski Most. And that is where the crossroads is. And to the left, was where the command post was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, very much, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we just -- the we just put it on the ELMO for a while until everyone sees where the high lighted spot is. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe she has copies for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And they are highlighted as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was going to highlight it for Your Honours, and I assume the Defence -- but I don't mind highlighting it to help out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've got my own highlighter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. He doesn't even want your highlighting, Ms. Korner. But I still say put it on the ELMO at least. We will see where the spot is. And then perhaps Ms. Gustin can do that while you continue with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can do that myself while he's just pointing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll hand one copy of it to the Defence and then three -- do Your Honours require three or just one between the three of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Just one copy is enough, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case -- well, as soon as the usher is finished, I'll hand it up. And I'll hand -- the Defence prefer to mark their own. That's for Their Honours. Thank you very much. And one copy each for the Defence and one for the Court. Your Honour, I think it better become -- there's actually a colour one which better become the original exhibit, I think, which is two -- whatever the maps are -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. That's one for Their Honours marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Three for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Just one is enough. And if we need more later on, I'm sure the Prosecution will make them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's just one for the registry, which is a colour copy, and then one copy each for the Defence. Your Honour, this was -- the colour one was produced by the -- I think the audiovisual -- the mapping section of our office. It may well be that was only lent to us. If necessary, we may have to substitute a black-and-white one as the original exhibit. We're just checking.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Sir, you were dealing with the SOS, the Serbian defence forces, before the break. And I just want to ask you this: Were they -- did they have their headquarters in any particular place in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did have a command post. But I learnt about that only in April, in the month of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where was their command post?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That command post was -- in Sanski Most was next to the Partizan sports hall, which had sports grounds behind it and playing fields and a fence, so that within that sports facility they had their headquarters, and that is where they gathered. On the floor above, there was the Sanski Most radio station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally for the moment on the SOS, this: Did you ever hear about a group calling itself the Serbian defence forces, the SOS, that went into Banja Luka in the beginning of April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of that group from Sanski Most that called itself the SOS, or rather, the Serbian defence forces. As for circumstances in Banja Luka, whether there was any such organisation there, I did not know, though I had heard that it -- that several paramilitary forces were active, such as the White Eagles and the SOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we move for a moment -- although we'll come back to the SOS role in the later events when we reach it. But you talked about how people were being dismissed and how the SOS to your knowledge was involved in one of those. When did the dismissals start? And can we deal first of all with the Bosniaks, the Muslims. When did they start to be dismissed?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dismissals of Muslims started already in April. I think after the 20th of April, I think. Maybe a little earlier, depending on the type of job and the significance of the position. And towards the end of April or the beginning of May or up to the 15th of May, all Muslims had been dismissed from their workplaces in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about Croats?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the situation was similar for Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the dismissals were ordered by whom?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it came from the Crisis Staff of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that -- we're going to see documents relating to the declaration of the Crisis Staff in April of 1992, but were there any dismissals before that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were dismissals.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in that event, before the Crisis Staff came into being, who was ordering the dismissals?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was the president of the municipality, Rasula, and Vrkes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how were they able to enforce the dismissals of employees? What control did they have over the companies involved?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Rasula was the president of the municipality, so he would call the directors of enterprises. Then there was the executive council. They also had a Serbian assembly, organs of authority. So I think that it was at meetings of those bodies that they adopted conclusions which they later implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You attended meetings of the assembly in your capacity as president of the court. Were you ever present at any meetings of the assembly when the dismissals were discussed or raised?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present at assembly meetings while the assembly was a joint one with delegates of all political parties participating, as a guest. And I was invited to attend those assembly meetings. However, when the deputies representing the SDS formed the Serbian assembly, I was no longer invited nor did I attend those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. That's the only point. Now, you said also that after the arrival of the SOS, people were leaving Sanski Most. In the period between the arrival of the SOS and your arrest at the end of May, how many people left Sanski Most roughly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that in April, pressure started to be brought to bear and there was propaganda, so that the people out of fear took buses that were organised by Sanatrans, the local transport company. They used them to leave Sanski Most and to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those pressures were getting stronger and stronger in the course of the month of April and also May. It is hard to say how many people actually left. However, I would frequently pass through settlements within Sanski Most municipality and the town itself, with a majority Bosniak population, and I would notice that there were less and less people, or rather, that windows were shut and the blinds closed in houses. And I also was able to see more and more organised bus transports for the population to leave. But it is hard to say how many people left before the beginning of the attack on Sanski Most, but quite a few left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of your --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of your fellow judges, did any of them leave as a result?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I think I mentioned once that there were ten judges working in the court, out of which another two judges were Bosniaks in addition to me, who was the president of the court. Two judges had already left in April, together with their families. They had left Sanski Most out of fear for their families. They told me that before they left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But of the judges who left, were they of -- were they all Muslims, or were there people of other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry -- all right. Was there a Serb who was working there but who was married to a Croat?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a lady judge of Serb ethnicity who had a mixed marriage, and they were the first to leave, in March. And it became clear to me already then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. By --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why she left, she didn't tell me, so I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about freedom of movement in Sanski Most? Did that become restricted in any way? And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already after the 19th of May -- no, the 19th of April - I'm sorry - 1992, there were checkpoints manned by the army and the police. At all intersections of roads, in front of buildings, of bridges. And already then there was a danger when people moved about. But it was only in May -- I can't remember now the exact date -- that the SDS Crisis Staff took a decision and proclaimed a curfew and prohibited movement from the evening until the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, what about weapons? Was there any arming of any particular ethnicity going on during this period, April/May or even before, of persons?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that citizens of Serb ethnicity in Sanski Most municipality with a few exceptions had been given arms, automatic weapons at that. And I know that weapons were distributed to them by the SDS. And also, I know that members of the 6th Krajina Brigade, as well as the reservists, that all of them had weapons. They didn't return them at all. On a number of occasions, I saw that some SDS representatives were bringing in weapons and distributing them among apartments. Of course this provoked fear among the other peoples. And in that fear, I think that also some Muslims and Croats purchased weapons. However, this was nowhere like the amount the Serbs had.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I just ask you a couple of questions about that answer. First of all, by the -- this period, April/May 1992, were there any Muslims or Croats still serving in the 6th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't, because the Muslims and Croats abandoned the 6th Krajina Brigade already in 1991, when this brigade was going to the battlefields in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about the weapons, the TO weapons? I think you told us yesterday that they were kept behind the police station. What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons of the Territorial Defence were by force, let me say, taken by the JNA. Or rather, already in 1991 - I don't remember the month - a law was passed in the federal assembly in Belgrade by summary procedure that the Territorial Defence in the republics had to be subordinated to the JNA. Using the provisions of this decision, I know- because I was an eyewitness - when trucks arrived from Banja Luka, military trucks then belonging to the 5th Corps at the time. And when the entirety of armaments were taken and loaded onto these trucks and driven off towards Palanka -- Lusci Palanka. These weapons were taken over by the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said that some Muslims and Croats had bought weapons. Who did they buy weapons from?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that these were individuals and in an insignificant number. They purchased them mostly from Serbs who were selling weapons. There were several channels. I heard about these already in those days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We will see that later on there was an order issued by the Crisis Staff that there should be a disarmament effectively of non-Serbs. This sale of weapons by Serbs to Muslims and Croats, did that in any way assist in the disarmament?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did, because the persons from whom they purchased weapons had exact information regarding the number of weapons, the type, and the person they had sold them to. So they simply took the money from these people. And when the disarming operation started, then they knew on the basis of that list who had what, and they would order those weapons to be surrendered. However, those persons were designated as extremists, who later ended up in prisons and detention camps and many of them were executed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move now, then, please, to the 20th of April of 1992. By that stage, first of all dealing with you, were there any other Muslim judges left at the Sanski Most court?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the last Muslim in the court, and I was the president of the court. I was expelled by force on the 15th of May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to come on to that.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to deal with the takeover, please. On the 20th of April, did the SDS then declare a Serbian municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: With it own assembly, headed by Rasula?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in addition, at about the same time did they declare that there was a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Although, the Crisis Staff had already been established before, but at this time it received an official proclamation by the Serb assembly. Its function, that was given to it by the assembly in conditions of war; and that it could issue decisions independently, like the -- like the assembly -- for the assembly, which the assembly would then confirm at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I know you since these events looked at documents that show that the Serb Crisis Staff in fact existed before, but at the time in Sanski Most were you aware that there was such a thing as the Serb Crisis Staff? Are you having a problem?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I just want this switched off. I'm sorry. Could you repeat the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll say it again. I'm sorry. I didn't realise. Of course, it's rather irritating. I know you've looked at documents since then that showed the existence of a Crisis Staff before its official declaration, but were you aware at the time, before April the 20th, that the SDS had created a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know, because these were difficult days for us Muslims and for other non-Serbs, because the events on the 17th of April and the 19th of April, that was the date when the police -- or rather, from the public security station, Bosniaks and Croats were expelled. So those employed policemen were expelled. And when they left and went to the municipality building. Then we were living in fear and expectation what would happen -- as to what would happen. At that time I knew that there was the SDS Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And just before we move to how the events progressed, were you -- had you ever heard of any kind of Crisis Staff being created in Banja Luka as a result of the Serb defence force's demands in Banja Luka? If you hadn't, say so straight away.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard and I knew that there was a Crisis Staff in Banja Luka. But I cannot tell you precisely when I found out about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before your arrest, had you heard of the creation of a regional Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, headed by Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you remember how you'd heard about it? Had you read about it, or had you heard it on the radio, or had somebody told you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was working in the court as the court president, and of course I did not want to leave my position until I could see what would happen to me. Although I was receiving threats, these were in written form and verbal, and these were threats on my life. I decided to stay at my position until the end. I had a conversation with the president of the municipality, Nedeljko Rasula, precisely in order to see his viewpoint and decision. On that occasion, I learnt from him that the question of the judiciary had not been resolved yet, and I also learnt that this matter was being resolved in Banja Luka. On that occasion, I also learnt that there was a Crisis Staff in Banja Luka which was dealing with these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Radoslav Brdjanin speak either in public at a rally or a meeting or on the radio or on television?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this was a long time ago -- it was ten years ago -- I think that I did hear him -- that I did hear some reports, rather, on the radio, but I don't recall that I watched it on television. I say I cannot recall, but it is possible that I did hear and see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when there was this declaration of the Serb municipality and the assembly and then the Crisis Staff, what happened as far as the various institutions in Sanski Most were concerned? For example, the SDK.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the decisions issued -- taken by the Crisis Staff, they were taking over certain positions and certain institutions. And in this vein -- I believe that it was sometime in April -- they came to the SDK without any announcement. Specifically it was Vrkes who came, who was at the time SDS president. He was accompanied by SOS members and the Serb police. They forcibly took over the SDK by -- by forcing Ankica Dobrijevic, who was a director and a Croat, by forcing her out of the building and by appointing a Serb lady in her place. They then directed payments, which until that time went through the public auditing service of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They redirected it, the payments, in another direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which was? Which direction?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Banja Luka and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
